To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two‐dimensional protein patterns obtained by two‐dimensional electrophoresis of breast cells are different for different cells and that the proteins found in the cells are differentially expressed.

(a) two‐dimensional gels of proteins isolated from human breast epithelium reveal differences in the expression of proteins among different cell types; (b) cytokeratins are differentially expressed in the normal cells, with the most abundant being cytokeratins of the 18 family, while cytokeratins in the tumor cells are more diverse; and (c) a composite human breast epithelial protein pattern was created that includes proteins commonly expressed in the different cells and proteins
the proteins of human breast epithelial cell types can be resolved and compared using two‐dimensionary gel electrophoresi.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of proteins that are common to or specific for particular subsets of cells in the human breast and with the characterization of the changes in the expression of these proteins during differentiation of the breast epithelium and during the development of breast cancer.
the identification of the gene products that define the normal and malignant human breast cell phenotype and the development of methods for their detection and quantitation.
the characterization of the proteins of normal and tumor cells from the human breast.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proteins of the normal and tumor breast cells are similar but not identical.

this study has demonstrated that the protein patterns of normal human breast cells in culture and in situ, and of tumor cells, are distinct from each other, and from the pattern of proteins in the normal human breast.
the two‐dimensional protein patterns obtained from normal breast tissue and from the breast tumor cells are different.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to identify proteins that are differentially expressed in normal and cancer cells, as well as proteins common to both cell types.
we are in the process of developing a protein pattern that will be used as a marker for breast epithelial cell differentiation.

we have developed a method for isolating cells from human breast tissue and milk, and have used these cells to produce protein patterns which are useful in the study of breast epithelial cell differentiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
two‐dimensional electrophoresis can be successfully applied to the analysis of proteins from human cells.

two‐dimensional electrophoresis can be used to compare the protein profiles of different cell types in the human breast in order to identify markers that will be used to study normal breast cell differentiation, and the dedifferentation or blocked differentiation characteristic to cancer.
there are many proteins that are differentially expressed among different types of cells in the breast.
